definition: Neural networks whose neurons communicate via discrete, time-stamped spikes rather than continuous activations, making time a first-class part of the computation.
A model of interconnected units (neurons) organized in layers that learns a mapping from inputs to outputs by adjusting connection weights.
The basic computational unit of a neural network; in a spiking network it integrates incoming signals and emits a spike when its membrane potential crosses a threshold.
A mathematical description of how a neuron's internal state evolves over time and when it produces a spike.
A simple spiking neuron model in which the membrane potential integrates input current while continuously leaking toward rest, firing a spike and resetting when it reaches threshold.
A two-variable spiking neuron model that reproduces a wide range of biological firing patterns while remaining computationally cheap.
The voltage difference across a neuron's membrane; its evolution toward a threshold determines when the neuron spikes.
A brief, discrete electrical event a neuron emits when its membrane potential crosses threshold; spikes are the signals exchanged in a spiking neural network.
The membrane potential level a neuron must reach to fire a spike, after which its potential is reset.
A short interval after a spike during which a neuron cannot fire again regardless of input.
The scheme by which real-valued information is converted into spike patterns over time, such as rate coding or temporal coding.
An encoding scheme in which information is carried by the firing rate (number of spikes per time window) of a neuron.
An encoding scheme in which information is carried by the precise timing of individual spikes rather than their average rate.
A weighted connection between two neurons through which spikes are transmitted, scaling the influence one neuron has on another.
The strength of a synapse, determining how much an incoming spike changes the receiving neuron's membrane potential.
A filtering operation applied to a neuron's input or spike train to shape how signals are integrated over time.
The biophysical benchmark neuron model in which a spike emerges from the coupled dynamics of voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channels rather than a threshold-and-reset rule.
An exponential integrate-and-fire neuron augmented with a slow adaptation current, reproducing most cortical firing patterns from a handful of parameters.
A spiking neuron model that replaces the hard firing threshold with an exponential term modeling realistic spike initiation.
A two-variable reduction of the Hodgkin-Huxley model that preserves the phase-plane geometry of excitability, making it a tractable caricature for qualitative analysis.
A conductance-based two-variable neuron with calcium and potassium currents that captures genuine biophysical excitability while remaining low-dimensional.
A neuron model that expresses the membrane voltage directly as a sum of response kernels triggered by past spikes, giving a closed-form trajectory between spikes.
An integrate-and-fire neuron with added noise, reproducing trial-to-trial variability and linking spiking to probabilistic inference.
A neuron model that treats the cell as a tree of electrically coupled membrane patches, so dendritic phenomena emerge from the spatial structure.
A family of synaptic learning rules in which the sign and size of a weight change depend on the relative timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes.
A lasting strengthening of a synapse following correlated activity, widely regarded as a cellular basis of learning and memory.
A lasting weakening of a synapse following particular activity patterns, the complement of long-term potentiation.
The foundational timing rule in which presynaptic-before-postsynaptic firing strengthens a synapse and the reverse order weakens it, with an effect that decays with the spike interval.
An extension of pair-based STDP that uses triplets of spikes with fast and slow traces, matching cortical data and recovering BCM-like behavior.
A timing rule that flips the classical window so causal pre-before-post order weakens the synapse, implementing predictive suppression of expected signals.
A timing rule that strengthens a synapse based on temporal proximity in either order, detecting synchrony and correlation rather than causal sequence.
A weight-dependent timing rule that scales each update by its distance from the weight bounds, yielding a stable single-peaked weight distribution without explicit normalization.
A plasticity rule gated on the low-pass-filtered postsynaptic membrane voltage, mirroring the NMDA receptor as a voltage-gated coincidence detector.
A three-factor learning rule in which local eligibility traces are converted into weight changes by a global reward signal, bridging Hebbian and reinforcement learning.
A rate-based plasticity law with a sliding modification threshold that provides built-in homeostasis and underlies ocular dominance formation.
A training technique that replaces the spike's zero derivative with a smooth stand-in so deep spiking networks can be trained by backpropagation.
A decaying memory at each synapse that marks recent pre-post coincidences as eligible for a later weight change once a modulatory signal arrives.

Designing silicon around the way the brain computes — event-driven, massively parallel, with synaptic memory placed next to the neurons that read it — so that sparse spiking activity translates directly into very low energy use.

Intel's research neuromorphic processor, a many-core chip that runs spiking networks entirely on-chip with programmable plasticity; its successor Loihi 2 adds a programmable neuron engine and graded spikes.
IBM's million-neuron neuromorphic chip, a 64-by-64 array of crossbar cores with fixed (non-plastic) synapses, clocked by a slow global tick and built for extreme energy efficiency.

The self-contained building block of a tiled neuromorphic chip: a crossbar of input axons and output neurons joined by a grid of programmable synapses, bundling its own memory, scheduler, and router so it can operate independently.

A processing style in which hardware does work only when a spike (an event) arrives, leaving idle regions of the network drawing almost no power, so energy tracks activity rather than a free-running clock.

A communication scheme for neuromorphic systems in which each spike is sent as a small packet carrying the address of its source or destination neuron, letting sparse events travel over a shared routing fabric.

A chip whose digital logic can be rewired after manufacture, built from look-up-table logic blocks and a programmable interconnect; researchers program it to emulate neuromorphic hardware and reprogram it as the model changes.

A massively parallel simulation platform built from many interconnected ARM cores that models large spiking networks in real time by exchanging spikes as small packets, used as a large-scale neuromorphic research machine.

The ability of a neuromorphic chip to adjust its own synapses while the network runs, using plasticity rules implemented in the hardware, so the network can keep adapting after deployment instead of being frozen after training.

An architectural principle of neuromorphic hardware in which each core stores its own synaptic and neuron state locally, so network parameters never travel across a shared memory bus — avoiding the data-movement bottleneck of conventional processors.

A design flow that compiles behavior written in a high-level language such as C or C++ into hardware, opening FPGA and neuromorphic implementation to engineers without a register-transfer-level hardware background.

The outer, six-layered sheet of the mammalian brain whose local circuit motif repeats strikingly uniformly across regions that process vision, touch, or planning, making it a natural target for reverse-engineering cortical computation.

The repeated local unit of the neocortex: a six-layered circuit motif that recurs across the cortical sheet, treated as a candidate generic unit of computation and a blueprint worth copying in neuromorphic hardware.

A class of spiking network, due to James E. Smith, built to mimic the neocortex: information is carried in the timing of spikes rather than a rate, and learning is local and biologically plausible through spike-timing-dependent plasticity rather than global backpropagation.

An alternative to Boolean algebra proposed by Smith in which the arrival time of a signal is the quantity computed on, letting ordinary digital logic gates be repurposed so that time itself becomes a free resource for encoding and processing information.

A technique for understanding a neuron model by reducing it to two slow variables and plotting its trajectories in a plane, so the firing threshold, excitability type, and all-or-nothing spiking can be read off the geometry.

A summary of the collective behavior of many neurons, giving the aggregate firing rate of a population; under conditions worked out in the dynamics literature a simple rate model captures it, scaling single-neuron descriptions up to decisions and memory retrieval.

Paired structures in the insect central brain, defined by their shape, location, and bilateral symmetry, that separate overlapping sensory inputs into distinct patterns and attach value to them; recent work suggests their output can carry a behavioral decision, not just an identity.

The thousands of intrinsic neurons of the mushroom body whose few-onto-many expansion decorrelates similar odor representations into sparse, distributed, distinct patterns well suited to associative learning.

The small set of neurons onto which many Kenyon cells converge, reading sparse odor patterns out as a valence — approach or avoidance — and, in recordings from walking cockroaches, firing ahead of episodes of locomotion.
The relatively few neurons that carry olfactory input from a sensory center such as the antennal lobe into the mushroom body, fanning out onto a much larger population of Kenyon cells.

The low-dimensional surface hidden inside the high-dimensional firing of a neural population: when the brain represents a variable with simple geometric structure, the population activity traces out that same shape, with the dimensionality of the behavior rather than the neuron count setting the form.

The phenomenon in which a contracting recurrent circuit driven by structured input locks onto the driving dynamics so its state becomes a function of recent input; formalized as a topological embedding, it can map a low-dimensional sensory manifold into a circuit's high-dimensional state space.

A recurrent network whose structured connectivity gives it a continuum of stable states forming a low-dimensional attractor; proposed as what a transient synchronization-based embedding crystallizes into once Hebbian plasticity reshapes it into the circuit's own connectivity.

The framework holding that the cortex performs inference by minimizing a free-energy quantity; it says the cortex infers but not why the inference yields the particular low-dimensional geometry seen in neural manifolds, a gap the synchronization account aims to fill.

A systematic method for compiling a mathematical description of a computation — a vector-valued function or dynamical system, plus neurobiological constraints — into a spiking neural network that approximates it, organised around three principles: representation, transformation, and dynamics.

The first NEF principle: a population of neurons represents a vector through encoding (each neuron fires according to its preferred direction, producing a tuning curve) and decoding (linear weights found by least squares recover an estimate of the value from the population's activity).

The second NEF principle: computation happens in the connections between populations by solving for decoders that approximate a function of the represented value, so a single set of synaptic weights both communicates a signal and computes a function of it.

In the NEF, a neuron's preferred-direction unit vector: the input direction for which the neuron fires most strongly, used together with a gain and bias to turn a represented value into that neuron's activity.
In the NEF, the set of linear weights — found by least-squares optimisation — that recover an estimate of the represented value (or a function of it) from a population's spiking activity.
The response profile of a neuron as a function of the represented value: how strongly it fires across the input space, peaking for inputs aligned with its preferred direction.

A compact, high-dimensional vector that stands for a concept: cheap to move around a network yet unpackable toward richer sensory or motor detail, much like a pointer in a program that refers to a larger structure.

A method for building neural models of high-level cognition that represents concepts as semantic pointers and combines them with algebraic operations, so structured, symbol-like information can be built and manipulated while staying grounded in neural activity.

The algebraic operation that ties a role to a filler and produces a new vector dissimilar to both inputs; in the Semantic Pointer Architecture it is implemented with circular convolution, which keeps the dimensionality fixed and has an approximate inverse for querying.
The algebraic operation that superposes several vectors by addition so the result stays similar to each part, representing a set or collection of semantic pointers.
A neural memory that maps the noisy result of an unbinding operation to the nearest known vocabulary vector, restoring a clean semantic pointer so multi-step symbol manipulation stays stable.

A family of approaches, including the Semantic Pointer Architecture, that represent structured information as high-dimensional vectors combined by binding and bundling, seeking the compositional behaviour of symbolic AI with the grounded, noise-tolerant character of neural representations.

An extension of semantic pointers to continuous quantities: a position in space is represented by raising a base vector to a fractional power (computed in the Fourier domain), so a representation can be shifted smoothly through space and read out as a heat map over candidate positions.
A large-scale functional brain model built on the Semantic Pointer Architecture that uses semantic pointers to perform a range of perceptual, memory, and motor tasks within a single spiking network.

A recurrent memory cell built around the mathematically optimal finite approximation to a continuous time delay, pairing a fixed linear memory system with a nonlinear read/write layer to give accurate, parameter-efficient memory of a rolling signal window.

The small linear recurrent system at the core of the LMU: derived by approximating an ideal delay with matched Pade approximants and projecting onto the shifted Legendre polynomials, its state holds the coefficients of a Legendre-polynomial expansion of the recent input window.
The neural simulator that implements the three NEF principles directly, so a described vector computation or dynamical system can be built and run as a spiking network.
A Python simulator for spiking neural networks in which models are written as equations with physical units and compiled to fast code (Stimberg, Brette & Goodman 2019).
A simulator for large networks of point neurons, designed for scalability on clusters and supercomputers (Gewaltig & Diesmann 2007).
A PyTorch library for training spiking neural networks with surrogate gradients and backpropagation through time (Eshraghian et al. 2023).
A PyTorch-based library of spiking neuron primitives for gradient-based and bio-inspired learning (Pehle & Pedersen 2021).
Intel's open-source software framework for neuromorphic computing, targeting Loihi 2 and conventional CPUs.
A simulator-independent Python API for describing spiking network models that can run on NEST, NEURON, Brian and neuromorphic hardware (Davison et al. 2009).
GPU-enhanced Neuronal Networks, a code-generation framework that runs spiking network simulations on GPUs.
A family of accelerated mixed-signal neuromorphic systems from Heidelberg in which analogue neuron circuits run about 1,000 times faster than biological real time.
Representing synaptic weights with few bits (for example 8 or fewer) on neuromorphic hardware, which can change learning and accuracy relative to floating-point simulation.
The maximum number of input synapses a hardware neuron or core can receive, a key constraint when mapping dense cortical connectivity to neuromorphic chips.
Converting input intensities into spike trains whose spikes occur randomly at a rate proportional to the intensity.
Encoding input strength in the time of a single spike, with stronger inputs firing earlier (time-to-first-spike).
Encoding a stimulus in the order in which a population of neurons fires its first spikes, which is invariant to overall intensity (Thorpe et al. 2001).
Representing a value by the joint activity of many neurons with overlapping tuning curves.
Emitting a spike only when the input has changed by more than a threshold since the last spike, as event cameras do per pixel.
An HTM encoder that maps a number to a block of contiguous active bits whose position moves with the value, so nearby values share bits.
An HTM encoder that assigns each value bucket a random set of active bits overlapping heavily with neighbouring buckets, needing no fixed range.
An encoder that represents a location with several periodic grid modules at different scales, giving unique, overlap-preserving SDRs for nearby locations.
An event camera whose pixels independently emit ON/OFF events when their brightness changes, producing sparse spike-like input.
For spike trains, the standard deviation of inter-spike intervals divided by their mean; about 1 for Poisson-like irregular firing.
The variance of spike counts divided by their mean across repeated trials; 1 for a Poisson process.
A plot of spike times (horizontal) for each neuron (vertical), the basic diagnostic view of a spiking network.
One synaptic event processed — a spike delivered to one target synapse; counting them estimates the work and energy of an SNN on neuromorphic hardware.
Simulated biological time divided by wall-clock time (or its inverse, depending on convention); a standard measure of simulator and hardware speed.
A failure mode in which recurrent excitation drives firing rates to their maximum because inhibition cannot keep up.
A neuron that never becomes active after learning, usually a sign of missing homeostasis.
A deliberately small first build of a cortical column model — a few hundred minicolumns and a few thousand neurons — used to validate mechanisms before scaling.

Numenta's algorithmic model of a neocortical layer: minicolumns of binary neurons that form sparse distributed representations (spatial pooler) and learn high-order sequences on distal dendritic segments (temporal memory).

The neuron model of Hawkins & Ahmad (2016): a proximal zone that drives firing plus many distal (and apical) dendritic segments, each a threshold coincidence detector whose activation puts the cell into a predictive, depolarised state.
In the HTM neuron, the synapses close to the soma (a minority, typically a few hundred) that carry feedforward input and can make the cell fire; all cells in a minicolumn share it.

In HTM, an independent stretch of basal dendrite modelled as a list of synapses onto other cells; if enough connected synapses are active (the activation threshold, roughly 10–16 in Numenta defaults) it fires an NMDA-spike-like event that makes the cell predictive.
In the HTM neuron, a dendritic segment on the apical tuft that receives top-down feedback and, like a distal segment, depolarises the cell without firing it; the least specified part of the model.
The HTM cell state between inactive and active: the cell is depolarised by an active dendritic segment, so if its minicolumn receives feedforward input it fires first and inhibits its neighbours.

A scalar in [0, 1] attached to each potential HTM synapse that models synapse formation; learning moves it up or down, and the synapse only has an effect (weight 1) when permanence exceeds the connection threshold.

An HTM synapse whose permanence is at or above the connected-permanence threshold (about 0.5 in temporal memory, 0.1–0.2 in typical spatial pooler settings); only connected synapses count towards overlap or segment activity.
The number of active connected synapses a distal segment needs to become active and make its cell predictive (activationThreshold in Numenta's code, typically about 13).
An HTM segment with at least minThreshold active potential (possibly unconnected) synapses; used to choose which cell and segment learn when a minicolumn bursts.

HTM's feedforward stage that turns an encoder's bit array into an SDR of active minicolumns with a fixed sparsity (about 2%) using overlap counting, k-winners inhibition, Hebbian permanence learning and boosting.
The fixed random subset of input bits that a spatial pooler minicolumn may ever connect to (a fraction potentialPct of its inputs); only synapses in the pool have permanences.
In the spatial pooler, the number of a minicolumn's connected synapses whose input bit is active, multiplied by its boost factor; the minicolumns with the highest overlap win inhibition.
A per-column multiplier in the spatial pooler, b = exp(−β(a − ⟨a⟩)), that raises the overlap of columns active less often than the target, keeping all columns in use (a homeostatic mechanism).

A moving average of how often a spatial pooler column has been active over the last dutyCyclePeriod steps; it drives boosting. The related overlap duty cycle tracks how often the column had enough input.

HTM's sequence-memory algorithm: within active minicolumns it activates the predicted cells (or bursts the whole minicolumn), and grows and reinforces distal segments so that context-specific cells predict the next input.
In HTM temporal memory, the activation of all cells in an active minicolumn because none of them was predicted; it signals surprise and is when new segments are learned.

The one cell per active minicolumn that learns at a given step in HTM temporal memory (a predicted cell, or during a burst the cell with the best matching segment or fewest segments); new synapses are grown to previous winner cells.
HTM's raw surprise measure: the fraction of currently active minicolumns that were not predicted at the previous step (0 = fully predicted, 1 = complete burst).
A post-processing of HTM anomaly scores (Ahmad et al. 2017) that compares a short moving average of recent scores with a Gaussian fitted to a long history and reports how far into the tail it lies.

A benchmark of labelled streaming time series (about 58 files) with a window-based scoring scheme that rewards early detection and penalises false positives (Lavin & Ahmad 2015); its reliability has been questioned.
Numenta's online book giving the reference description and pseudocode of SDRs, encoders, the spatial pooler and temporal memory.
Numenta's original open-source HTM library (Python 2.7 with a C++ core), now in maintenance mode.
A community-maintained continuation of NuPIC's C++ core with Python 3 bindings; the most practical way to run HTM today.

One of the six horizontal strata (L1–L6) of the neocortical sheet, each with a characteristic mix of cells, inputs and output targets; L4 receives core thalamic input, L2/3 projects to other cortical areas, L5 projects subcortically and L6 back to the thalamus.
Cortex, such as primary motor cortex, in which layer 4 is strongly reduced or not visible in standard stains; mouse motor cortex still contains a thin L4-like population.
The branched end of a pyramidal neuron's apical dendrite, often lying in layer 1, where it receives top-down feedback and matrix-thalamic input.
A narrow vertical chain of roughly 80–120 neurons (more in primate V1), spaced about 30–60 µm apart depending on species and area; the unit called a 'column' in HTM.
A cylinder of cortex roughly 300–600 µm across whose neurons share a receptive-field property (e.g. the same whisker or eye), containing on the order of 10⁴ neurons and many minicolumns.
The part of rodent primary somatosensory cortex where L4 forms discrete clusters (barrels), one per whisker; the clearest anatomically bounded example of a cortical column.
The main excitatory neuron of the cortex, with a triangular soma, basal dendrites, a long apical dendrite and an axon that usually leaves the local area; typically receives thousands of synapses.
A star-shaped excitatory neuron without a prominent apical dendrite, found in L4 of some primary sensory areas, that receives core thalamic input and projects locally.
A locally projecting inhibitory (GABAergic) neuron; about 15–30% of cortical neurons, mostly in the PV, SST and VIP classes.
A fast-spiking inhibitory neuron (basket or chandelier cell) that targets pyramidal somata or axon initial segments and provides fast feedforward and feedback inhibition.
An inhibitory neuron, often a Martinotti cell, that targets pyramidal dendrites including apical tufts in L1 and is recruited by facilitating synapses during sustained activity.
An SST-expressing interneuron whose axon ascends to layer 1 to inhibit the apical tufts of pyramidal neurons.
An inhibitory neuron expressing vasoactive intestinal peptide that mainly inhibits SST interneurons, thereby disinhibiting pyramidal dendrites.
Increase in a neuron's excitability caused by inhibiting its inhibitors, as when VIP cells suppress SST cells and release pyramidal dendrites from inhibition.
The rule that a neuron releases the same transmitter at all its output synapses, so it is either excitatory or inhibitory; in models, the sign of a weight belongs to the presynaptic neuron.
A paired forebrain structure whose nuclei relay sensory signals to the cortex and exchange driving and modulatory signals with almost every cortical area.
In Sherman and Guillery's classification, a glutamatergic input with large proximal terminals, ionotropic receptors and depressing synapses that carries the information a neuron relays.

An input with small distal terminals, often metabotropic receptors and facilitating synapses that sets the gain or mode of a neuron rather than its receptive field; L6 feedback to thalamus is the classic example.
A thin shell of GABAergic neurons around the thalamus, excited by thalamocortical and corticothalamic collaterals, that inhibits thalamic relay cells.
Thalamic nuclei, such as the LGN or VPM, that relay driver input from subcortical sources to primary cortical areas.
Thalamic nuclei, such as the pulvinar or POm, whose driver input comes from cortical layer 5 and which relay it to other cortical areas.
A route between cortical areas that runs from layer 5 of one area through a higher-order thalamic nucleus to another area, in parallel with direct cortico-cortical connections.
Jones's division of thalamic relay cells into core cells projecting focally to middle layers and matrix cells projecting diffusely to superficial layers, especially L1.
The modulatory projection from layer 6 pyramidal cells back to the thalamic nucleus that feeds the area and to the thalamic reticular nucleus.

Mountcastle's proposal that the neocortex is built from a repeated columnar circuit performing a common operation, with areas differing mainly in their connections; supported by rewiring experiments but challenged by regional differences.

The proposal (Douglas, Martin & Whitteridge 1989; Douglas & Martin 1991) that a stereotyped circuit of recurrently connected excitatory and inhibitory neurons across layers is repeated throughout neocortex.
The amplification of weak thalamic input by recurrent connections among cortical excitatory neurons, balanced by inhibition, a central feature of the canonical microcircuit.
A theory in which each level of a hierarchy predicts the activity of the level below and only the prediction errors are passed upward (Rao & Ballard 1999).
The difference between an input and a prediction of it; in predictive coding it drives inference and learning and is proposed to be carried by superficial pyramidal cells.
In predictive coding and the free-energy framework, scaling prediction errors by their expected reliability (inverse variance).
Neural activity evoked when sensory input differs from what an animal's own movement predicts, reported in mouse visual cortex layer 2/3 (Keller & Mrsic-Flogel 2018 review).

A full-density spiking model of the microcircuit under 1 mm² of early sensory cortex: about 77,000 LIF neurons in eight populations (excitatory and inhibitory in L2/3, L4, L5 and L6) with about 0.3 billion synapses (Potjans & Diesmann 2014).
A network model with the real number of neurons and synapses of the tissue it represents, avoiding the distortions of correlations and fluctuations that downscaling introduces.
The EPFL project, launched in 2005 under Henry Markram, that built biophysically detailed digital reconstructions of rodent neocortical tissue (Markram et al. 2015).
A data-driven simulation model of brain tissue assembled from measured cell morphologies, electrical types, densities and connection rules.
A class of neurons defined by the shape of their dendrites and axons; Markram et al. (2015) used 55 m-types.
A class of neurons defined by their firing behaviour in response to current injection (e.g. continuous accommodating, bursting).
A population-level model describing the average activity of large neuron groups instead of individual spikes, used to analyse network regimes.
Strengthening a synapse when its presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons are active together ("cells that fire together wire together"), after Hebb's 1949 postulate.
A normalised Hebbian rule, Δw = η·y·(x − y·w), whose weights converge to the first principal component of the input instead of growing without bound (Oja 1982).
The function giving the STDP weight change as a function of the spike-time difference Δt = t_post − t_pre, typically potentiation for Δt > 0 and depression for Δt < 0 decaying over ~20 ms.
An exponentially decaying variable incremented at each spike, used to implement STDP online: the presynaptic trace is read at postsynaptic spikes and vice versa.
Slow processes that keep a neuron's activity within a target range despite learning, such as synaptic scaling, adaptive thresholds and intrinsic plasticity.
Multiplicative up- or down-scaling of all of a neuron's excitatory synapses in response to prolonged changes in its activity (Turrigiano et al. 1998).
A firing threshold that increases each time the neuron spikes and slowly decays, discouraging any single neuron from dominating; used in Diehl & Cook (2015).
Activity-dependent changes in a neuron's own excitability (ion channel properties) rather than its synapses.
Rescaling a neuron's incoming weights to a fixed total after learning, a simple stabiliser for Hebbian and STDP learning.
Inhibition between neighbouring neurons of the same layer, usually via interneurons, that sharpens responses and creates competition.
A competitive circuit in which only the most strongly driven neuron (or a few) stays active while inhibition silences the others; soft WTA allows graded competition.
A competition rule that keeps exactly the k most strongly driven units active and silences the rest, an abstraction of fast inhibition used to produce fixed-sparsity codes.
The approximate cancellation of excitatory and inhibitory input to cortical neurons, which keeps activity irregular and sensitive to input fluctuations.
A network regime with low, irregular (Poisson-like) firing and weak correlations between neurons, characteristic of awake cortex and of balanced network models.
A code in which a small fraction of many units is active and meaning is carried by which units are active, giving high capacity and noise tolerance.
The number of active bits two sparse distributed representations share; a measure of their similarity.
The probability that a random SDR shares at least θ active bits with a stored one, which falls extremely fast with SDR size and sparsity (Ahmad & Hawkins 2016).
Several SDRs can be stored as their union (OR) and a new SDR tested for membership by overlap, with an error rate that grows as the union fills up.
Recognising an SDR by connecting to only a small random subset of its active bits, which still gives a low false-match rate — how a dendritic segment can detect a pattern with ~10–20 synapses.
The smallest constant input current that makes a neuron fire; for a LIF neuron it equals (threshold − resting potential) / membrane resistance.
The firing rate of a neuron as a function of constant input current; zero below rheobase and rising (for LIF, saturating at 1 / refractory period) above it.
τm = RC, the time over which a neuron's membrane potential relaxes back toward rest; it sets how long the neuron integrates its input (typically 10–30 ms in cortical neurons).
Updating a differential equation in fixed steps, x(t+dt) = x(t) + dt · dx/dt; simple and common in SNN simulators but inaccurate when dt approaches the model's fastest time constant.
The most common firing pattern of cortical excitatory neurons: spikes with adapting intervals under constant input; in the Izhikevich model a = 0.02, b = 0.2, c = −65, d = 8.
The firing pattern of parvalbumin-positive inhibitory interneurons: high-frequency spikes with little adaptation; in the Izhikevich model a = 0.1, b = 0.2, c = −65, d = 2.
Firing in clusters of several closely spaced spikes separated by pauses, as in intrinsically bursting and chattering cortical neurons.
In the Hodgkin–Huxley model, a number between 0 and 1 (m, h, n) giving the fraction of ion-channel gates in the open state, obeying first-order voltage-dependent kinetics.
A membrane protein that lets specific ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻) cross the membrane; voltage- and ligand-gated channels produce spikes and synaptic currents.
A synapse modelled as a conductance g(t) so that the current g(t)·(E_rev − V) depends on the membrane potential and reverses sign at the reversal potential.
A synapse modelled as an injected current independent of the membrane potential; simpler and cheaper than the conductance-based form, used in many network models.
The membrane potential at which a channel's net current is zero, e.g. about 0 mV for AMPA/NMDA and about −70 to −80 mV for GABA_A synapses.
A fast glutamate receptor (decay of a few ms) carrying most fast excitatory synaptic current.
A glutamate receptor with slow kinetics (tens of ms) blocked by Mg²⁺ at rest, so it conducts only when the membrane is depolarised; it underlies NMDA spikes and much synaptic plasticity.
Receptors for the inhibitory transmitter GABA: fast ionotropic GABA_A (chloride, a few to ~10 ms) and slow metabotropic GABA_B (potassium, hundreds of ms).
Changes in synaptic efficacy over tens to hundreds of ms caused by recent presynaptic activity — depression from resource depletion or facilitation — modelled by Tsodyks and Markram (1997).
A local regenerative depolarisation in a thin dendrite, lasting tens of ms, triggered when enough nearby synapses are activated together; proposed as the biological basis of HTM dendritic segments.
A prolonged depolarisation (tens to hundreds of ms) in a dendrite or soma, for example after an NMDA spike, that raises the neuron's excitability.
A somatic spike that travels back into the dendrites, signalling to synapses that the neuron fired; important for STDP and for BAC firing.

Backpropagation-activated calcium spike firing: coincidence of a back-propagating spike with apical input triggers a dendritic calcium spike and a somatic burst in layer 5 pyramidal neurons (Larkum et al. 1999).
The idea that a pyramidal neuron computes like a two-layer network: dendritic branches apply sigmoidal nonlinearities to their inputs and the soma sums the results (Poirazi, Brannon & Mel 2003).
The theory that every neocortical column learns complete models of objects using reference frames, and that columns vote to reach a consensus percept (Hawkins et al. 2017, 2019; Hawkins 2021).
A coordinate system in which locations are represented; in the Thousand Brains Theory each column stores objects as features at locations in object-centric reference frames.
A reference frame attached to an object, so that locations of its features do not change when the object or observer moves.
A neuron in the entorhinal cortex that fires at the vertices of a triangular lattice tiling the environment, discovered by Hafting et al. (2005); proposed to have analogues in cortical columns.
A hippocampal neuron that fires when an animal is in a particular location of its environment (O'Keefe & Dostrovsky 1971).
A group of grid cells sharing the same grid spacing and orientation; several modules at different scales together encode location uniquely over a large range.
Updating an estimate of one's location by integrating self-motion (velocity and direction) over time, without external landmarks.

A hypothetical neuron, proposed by Hawkins et al. (2019), that represents the relative displacement between two locations, for example between parts of a composite object; not yet observed experimentally.
A pairing of a sensed feature with the location where it was sensed on an object; the unit of object models in the Thousand Brains Theory.
Recognising an object by combining a sequence of sensations with the movements between them, narrowing the set of objects consistent with all feature-location observations.
The proposal that columns sensing different parts of an object share their candidate objects through long-range lateral connections so all columns quickly settle on the consensus.
Horizontal connections, prominent in layers 2/3 and 5, linking columns across a cortical region; proposed in the Thousand Brains Theory to carry the votes between columns.
The open-source sensorimotor learning system of the Thousand Brains Project, built from learning modules and sensor modules that communicate via the Cortical Messaging Protocol.
The open-source research initiative, launched in 2024 by Numenta researchers, that develops Monty and sensorimotor AI based on the Thousand Brains Theory.
In Monty, the unit corresponding to a cortical column: it receives features at poses, learns structured object models, and votes with other learning modules.
In Monty, the component that turns raw sensor data from a small patch into features with a pose in a common format for learning modules.
The common message format in Monty — features or object IDs together with a location and orientation (pose) — used between sensor modules, learning modules and motor systems.
A class of neurons that share consistent morphology, firing behaviour, gene expression and connectivity, such as layer 5 pyramidal cells or PV basket cells.
A technique that records a neuron's electrical behaviour with a patch pipette, fills it to reconstruct its shape, and sequences its RNA, so all three views of cell type come from the same cell.
A neuron class defined by clustering single-cell RNA sequencing data, i.e. by which genes the cells express.
A shared vocabulary (Ascoli et al. 2008) for describing cortical interneurons by morphology, molecular markers and firing pattern.
The Allen Institute's open database of mouse and human neuron recordings, morphologies and fitted GLIF and biophysical models.
A knowledge base of over 120 rodent hippocampal neuron types with their morphology, markers, firing and fitted Izhikevich parameters.
A family of LIF models extended with after-spike currents and an adaptive threshold, fitted by the Allen Institute to individual neurons to classify cell types.
A public database of published computational neuroscience models with their source code, searchable by cell type, channel and simulator.
Blue Brain's open-source Python tool for fitting neuron model parameters to electrophysiological features with multi-objective optimisation.
Fitting a neuron model by matching summary features of recordings (spike count, adaptation, AP width, sag and so on) rather than the raw voltage trace.
The lengthening of interspike intervals during a constant stimulus, caused by slow potassium currents that build up with each spike.
A firing class that starts a current step with a burst of spikes and then fires single spikes; typical of thick-tufted layer 5 and CA3 pyramidal cells.
A firing class of repeated high-frequency bursts at 20-80 Hz, found in some superficial pyramidal cells.
A firing class that responds to small currents, adapts and can rebound-burst after hyperpolarisation via T-type calcium current; typical of SST interneurons.
A neuron class defined by its response to injected current: regular spiking, bursting, fast spiking and so on. Also called an e-type.
How much a hyperpolarised membrane potential rebounds back toward rest during a step, a measure of the h-current.
A cortical pyramidal cell whose axon stays within the telencephalon, projecting to other cortical areas and the striatum; found in layers 2 to 6.
A thick-tufted layer 5 pyramidal cell whose axon leaves the telencephalon for the brainstem, spinal cord and thalamus; the cortex's main output cell.
A superficial cortical pyramidal neuron that fires sparsely, connects densely to its neighbours and projects to other cortical areas.
A large layer 5b pyramidal cell with a long apical dendrite and big tuft in layer 1; it bursts when basal and tuft inputs coincide (BAC firing).
A slow, regenerative dendritic event carried by voltage-gated calcium channels, generated near the apical bifurcation of layer 5 pyramidal cells.
The detailed, multi-objective-fitted multi-compartment model of a rat thick-tufted layer 5 pyramidal cell (Hay et al. 2011) that reproduces somatic firing and BAC firing.
The idea that a neuron's spike train carries two signals at once: event rate (bottom-up input) and burst fraction (coincident top-down input).
Inhibition triggered by the same input that excites a cell, arriving a millisecond or two later, which narrows the time window for integration.
A layer 4 excitatory cell with a small apical dendrite, intermediate between a spiny stellate and a pyramidal cell.
Scaling of cortical response strength without changing selectivity; layer 6 corticothalamic cells exert it on the other layers through translaminar interneurons.
A layer 6 pyramidal cell that projects back to the thalamic nucleus feeding its cortical area, with weak, facilitating, modulatory synapses, and back up to layer 4.
A fast-spiking interneuron, usually parvalbumin-positive, whose axon forms baskets of synapses around the somata of pyramidal cells.
A single-compartment conductance model of a fast-spiking hippocampal interneuron (Wang & Buzsaki 1996) whose inhibitory networks synchronise at gamma frequency.
Rhythmic population activity at roughly 30-80 Hz, generated by fast-spiking PV interneurons interacting with each other (ING) or with pyramidal cells (PING).
A gamma-rhythm mechanism in which pyramidal cells excite interneurons, whose inhibition then silences the pyramidal cells until it wears off, each cycle.
A high-voltage-activated, fast-deactivating potassium channel that lets fast-spiking interneurons repolarise quickly and fire at hundreds of Hz.
A direct channel between two cells that passes current both ways; PV and SST interneurons form separate electrically coupled networks.
An interneuron whose synapses all target the axon initial segments of pyramidal cells, in vertical rows of boutons called cartridges.
The first stretch of axon next to the soma, densely packed with sodium channels, where action potentials are normally initiated.
Inhibition between pyramidal cells relayed by Martinotti cells, which appears only when the first pyramidal cell fires at high rate because the synapse onto the Martinotti cell facilitates.
The reduction of a neuron's response when a stimulus extends beyond its receptive field, partly mediated by SST interneurons.
A network whose recurrent excitation alone would be unstable and is held stable by fast feedback inhibition; it responds paradoxically to direct drive of its inhibitory cells.
A small, late-spiking interneuron with a dense axon that releases GABA into the surrounding space, giving slow GABA-A and GABA-B inhibition to all nearby cells.
Release of a transmitter into the extracellular space so that it acts on receptors of many nearby cells rather than at one synapse.
A metabotropic GABA receptor that opens potassium channels through G proteins, producing slow inhibition lasting hundreds of milliseconds.
A firing pattern with a long delay before the first spike at threshold current, caused by a slowly inactivating A-type potassium current.
Embryonic structures where cortical interneurons are born: PV and SST cells come from the medial, VIP and neurogliaform cells mostly from the caudal ganglionic eminence.
The third major family of cortical interneurons, defined by the ionotropic serotonin receptor 5HT3a; includes VIP and most neurogliaform cells.
A synapse whose response grows with repeated presynaptic spikes, so it transmits bursts and sustained trains far better than single spikes; pyramidal-to-SST synapses are the classic cortical example.
The VIP → SST → pyramidal cell chain: VIP cells inhibit SST cells and so release pyramidal dendrites from inhibition, carrying context and behavioural state into the circuit.
The hippocampal pathway entorhinal cortex → dentate gyrus → CA3 → CA1, with three successive excitatory synapses.
The projection from entorhinal cortex layer 2 (and 3) to the dentate gyrus, CA3 and CA1; the hippocampus's main input.
A 4-12 Hz oscillation prominent in the hippocampus during movement and REM sleep, which organises the timing of place-cell spikes.
A brief, synchronous population burst from CA3 that drives a 150-250 Hz ripple in CA1 during rest and sleep, often replaying place-cell sequences.
The hippocampus's main output neuron, often a place cell, receiving CA3 input proximally and entorhinal input on its distal tuft.
A one-shot plasticity rule in CA1: a dendritic plateau potential potentiates all inputs active within a window of seconds around it, creating a place field in a single trial.
The shift of a place cell's spikes to earlier phases of the theta rhythm as an animal moves through its place field.
A burst of 2-6 action potentials of decreasing amplitude fired by hippocampal pyramidal cells on a dendritic calcium event.
A hippocampal pyramidal cell with dense recurrent connections and intrinsic bursting, the basis of autoassociative memory models.
A two-compartment reduction of Traub's CA3 neuron in which one coupling conductance moves the cell between bursting and regular spiking.
Axon branches by which CA3 pyramidal cells excite one another, forming the network thought to store and complete memories.
A recurrent network that stores patterns in its weights and recalls a whole pattern from a partial or noisy cue (pattern completion).
Recall of a complete stored pattern from a partial cue, attributed to the CA3 recurrent network.
The axon of a dentate granule cell, making few but very strong, facilitating 'detonator' synapses onto CA3 pyramidal cells.

aliases: granule cell of the dentate gyrus
definition: A small, very sparsely active excitatory neuron of the dentate gyrus that expands entorhinal input into a sparse code.
Making similar input patterns less similar in their neural representation, typically by a sparse expansion code; attributed to the dentate gyrus.
The birth of new neurons in the adult brain, notably dentate granule cells in rodents; its extent in humans is debated.
A hippocampal SST interneuron in stratum oriens whose axon inhibits the distal tufts of CA1 pyramidal cells; its h-current makes it fire at theta rates.
A cation current opened by hyperpolarisation (HCN channels) that produces sag, rebound and theta-range resonance.
A layer 2 medial entorhinal neuron with theta resonance from a strong h-current; many are grid cells and project via the perforant path.
Rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential below spike threshold, produced by interacting currents such as Ih and persistent sodium.
A grid-cell model in which grid fields arise from interference between velocity-controlled oscillators; largely superseded by attractor models.
A neuron's preference for inputs at a particular frequency, seen as a peak in its impedance; theta resonance is typical of entorhinal stellate cells.
The theory that the cerebellum is a supervised learner: granule cells expand mossy fibre input, Purkinje cells act as perceptrons, and climbing fibres provide the error signal.
The T-shaped axon of a cerebellar granule cell, running along the folium and making weak synapses on hundreds of Purkinje cells.
The axon of an inferior olive neuron; each Purkinje cell receives exactly one, which triggers complex spikes and acts as a teaching signal.
Long-term depression of parallel fibre-Purkinje cell synapses when parallel fibre and climbing fibre activity coincide; the core plasticity of the Marr-Albus-Ito theory.
The large inhibitory output neuron of the cerebellar cortex, with a flat dendritic tree receiving about 100,000+ parallel fibre synapses and one climbing fibre.
The all-or-none burst-like response of a Purkinje cell to its climbing fibre, about 1 Hz, which triggers dendritic calcium and plasticity.
An ordinary sodium spike of a Purkinje cell, fired spontaneously at tens of Hz and modulated by parallel fibre and interneuron input.
A sodium current that flows briefly during repolarisation after a spike, enabling the high-frequency firing of Purkinje and other fast neurons.
The 1994 detailed multi-compartment model of the cerebellar Purkinje cell, with 1,600 compartments and ten channel types.
The most numerous neuron in the brain: a tiny excitatory cell with about four mossy fibre inputs whose axon becomes a parallel fibre.
Mapping inputs onto a much larger population with sparse random connectivity, making patterns more separable for a downstream linear readout.
An inhibitory interneuron of the cerebellar granular layer that controls granule cell activity by feedforward, feedback and tonic inhibition.
Albus's (1975) cerebellum-inspired associative memory for control, using coarse-coded expansion of inputs and a trained linear readout.
A brainstem nucleus of electrically coupled, oscillating neurons that send climbing fibres to the cerebellum.
An excitatory thalamic neuron that relays sensory or cortical input to cortex in tonic mode, or fires bursts after hyperpolarisation.
A low-threshold calcium current that is inactivated at rest and de-inactivated by hyperpolarisation; it produces rebound bursts in thalamic and other neurons.
The firing mode of a hyperpolarised thalamic relay cell, which answers depolarisation with a low-threshold calcium spike and a burst; in tonic mode it fires single spikes instead.
A burst of spikes fired when a neuron is released from hyperpolarisation, typically through a de-inactivated T-type calcium current.
An LIF neuron plus one slow T-current gating variable (Smith et al. 2000), the cheapest model with both tonic and burst modes of thalamic relay cells.
A 7-14 Hz waxing-and-waning oscillation of light sleep, generated by the thalamic reticular nucleus and thalamocortical relay cells.
A GABAergic neuron of the thin shell around the thalamus that receives thalamocortical and corticothalamic collaterals and inhibits relay cells.
Crick's (1984) proposal that the thalamic reticular nucleus directs attention by controlling which thalamic relay channels reach cortex.
A set of subcortical nuclei (striatum, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra) that select actions and learn from reward.
The input nucleus of the basal ganglia, receiving cortical and thalamic glutamate and midbrain dopamine; made mostly of medium spiny neurons.
The basal ganglia route from D1 striatal neurons to the output nuclei that releases actions; the indirect route from D2 neurons via GPe and STN suppresses them.
A transmitter such as dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline or acetylcholine, released by small populations with widespread axons, that changes the state, gain or plasticity of large circuits.
A brainstem nucleus of noradrenergic pacemaker neurons whose bursts signal salience and arousal across the brain.
The GABAergic projection neuron that makes up about 95% of the striatum, with up and down states, a high threshold and D1 or D2 dopamine receptors.

Alternation of a neuron's membrane potential between a hyperpolarised quiet state and a depolarised state near threshold, driven by synchronous input; typical of striatal and cortical neurons in slow-wave states.
A midbrain neuron of the VTA or substantia nigra that fires as a slow pacemaker and bursts or pauses to signal reward prediction errors.
The difference between received and predicted reward; signalled by phasic dopamine firing.
A reinforcement learning method that updates value predictions using the error δ = r + γV(s′) − V(s); dopamine firing resembles δ.
A neuron that fires rhythmically without synaptic input, driven by its intrinsic currents; dopamine, Purkinje and GPe neurons are examples.
The output neuron of the retina; about 40 types each encode a different visual feature in spike trains sent along the optic nerve.
A light-sensitive retinal cell (rod or cone) that hyperpolarises to light and signals with graded, not spiking, transmitter release.
A non-spiking retinal interneuron that carries photoreceptor signals to ganglion cells, split into ON and OFF, sustained and transient types.
An inhibitory retinal interneuron, with over 40 types, that shapes timing and computes features such as motion direction.
A receptive field whose centre and surround have opposite effects, e.g. an ON-centre cell excited by central light and inhibited by surrounding light.
A statistical spiking model with stimulus, spike-history and coupling filters feeding an exponential rate; Pillow et al. (2008) used it to predict retinal ganglion cell spikes.
A model of a sensory neuron as a linear filter on the stimulus followed by a static nonlinearity and (often) Poisson spiking.
A neuron whose axon drives skeletal muscle fibres; each one with its fibres forms a motor unit.
One motor neuron together with all the muscle fibres it innervates.
Motor neurons are recruited from smallest to largest as drive increases, because small cells reach threshold first.
Non-inactivating sodium and calcium currents, often dendritic and neuromodulator-dependent, that amplify input and produce plateau potentials in motor neurons.
A star-shaped glial cell that wraps synapses, clears glutamate, buffers potassium and responds to activity with slow calcium signals.
The non-neuronal cells of the nervous system: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and others; about as numerous as neurons in the human brain.
The idea that a synapse includes an astrocyte process alongside the pre- and postsynaptic elements, able to sense and modulate transmission.
A two-variable model of IP3-receptor-mediated calcium release from internal stores (Li & Rinzel 1994), the core of most astrocyte calcium models.
A glial cell that wraps central axons in myelin, speeding conduction; activity-dependent myelination can tune conduction delays.
The brain's resident immune cells, which survey tissue and prune synapses during development.
Release of signalling molecules (glutamate, ATP, D-serine) by glia, especially astrocytes; its physiological role is debated.
